title: The golden deer
hookLine: a deer too beautiful to be real grazes by the hut; Hindus have a name for that shine: maya
last: SMARANA: REMEMBERING GOD, EVEN THROUGH FEAR.

cards: Near Panchavati, Maricha changes shape. Valmiki enjoys describing what he becomes: a golden body dotted with silver, horns tipped with jewels, a face of rubies and sapphires, ears like blue lotuses.

It wanders near the hut, nibbling leaves, running a little, coming back, lying down nearby as if it had all the time in the world. The other deer of the forest smell something wrong and keep their distance.

teach.b: Sita calls to Rama and Lakshmana, amazed, and they come. Lakshmana looks for a moment and says it plainly. This is Maricha.
Kings who came hunting in this forest have been killed by him in disguise. There's no deer like this anywhere on earth. It's a trick.
Sita, the text says, is captivated. She asks Rama to catch it, alive if he can, to keep in the palace when the exile ends.

teach.h: CATCH IT, OR BRING THE SKIN.
teach.b: If he can't, bring back the golden skin. Rama is captivated too, but not naive. If it's real, he says, it's a wonder.
If it's Maricha, it's a rakshasa who has killed people, and I should deal with it anyway.
Either way, I'll go. Guard Sita. Don't leave her for a moment.
Nobody here is foolish, and still every reasonable choice walks into Ravana's plan. Hindu teachers have long read this deer as a picture of maya, one of the tradition's biggest words.

teach.h: MAYA: THE SHINE OF WHAT PASSES.
teach.b: Maya is the power that makes the passing world look like all there is, so its shine pulls the mind away from what lasts. Later tellings even call the deer the maya-mriga, the illusion-deer.
And Vedanta names the answer: viveka, discernment, the habit of asking what lasts and what passes. Lakshmana has it in a single look. Sita and Rama, good and wise, are pulled by the gold.
Maya doesn't need you to be a fool. It only needs you looking at the shine, and not at the forest around it.

how: The golden deer is a familiar scene in Ramayana painting and Ramlila performance, and some Hindu teachers use the mayamriga, the illusion-deer, as a picture of maya and of the discernment (viveka) that sees through it.

o: a gift of the forest gods to cheer the exiles
Maricha in disguise, too beautiful to be real
a sacred deer that Sita once raised in Ayodhya

games.q: the deer and the teaching — tap the pairs.
p: asking: does it last, or pass?

s: Lakshmana is fooled by the deer
he says at once it's Maricha in disguise.
teachers read the golden deer as a picture of maya
later tellings call it the mayamriga, the illusion-deer: the shine that pulls the mind from what lasts.
maya means the world is fake and nothing in it matters
many teachers read maya as the world's shine hiding what lasts, not as 'nothing matters'. the answer is viveka, seeing clearly.

games.q: a sneaker drop: $300, 'only 2 hours left!' your friend says it's a must. thinking like Lakshmana, what's the first move?
o: ask it the viveka question: does this last, or pass?
buy it before it's gone; you can think after.
decide wanting anything is maya, so want nothing ever.
games.why: viveka isn't refusing everything. it's seeing the shine for what it is before you chase it, as Lakshmana did.

practice: Here's a simple viveka practice Hindu teachers give. Think of something shiny you want right now: a purchase, a feed you can't stop scrolling, a plan that looks too good. Picture it golden and bright.
Then ask it the old question, gently: do you last, or do you pass? Don't argue with the answer. Just notice what a calm part of you sees, the way Lakshmana saw.
Then come back to the plain, ordinary breath, which is here, and real.

wordCard.voice: The golden deer. Maricha in disguise, too beautiful to be real: maya with four legs. Lakshmana sees through it, Sita longs for it, and Rama goes after it.

orig.note: Sanskrit māyāmṛga: illusion-deer, a name later tellings give the golden deer.

carryVoice: Your line: maya shines; viveka sees through. Lakshmana saw the deer for what it was. Day five hundred sixty-eight, done.
